description: Expro Ltd provides energy services in North and Latin America, Europe and Sub-Saharan Africa, the Middle East and North Africa, and the Asia-Pacific. It provides well construction products and service
beta_warnings: Low R² (0.12) — the market explains little of the return variance
description_full: Expro Ltd provides energy services in North and Latin America, Europe and Sub-Saharan Africa, the Middle East and North Africa, and the Asia-Pacific. It provides well construction products and services, such as technology solutions in tubular running services, tubular products, cementing, drilling, and wellbore cleanup; and well management services comprising well flow management, subsea well access, and well intervention and integrity solutions. The company serves exploration and production companies in onshore and offshore environments. Expro Ltd was formerly known as Expro Group Holdings N.V. Expro Ltd was founded in 1938 and is based in Houston, Texas.
ceo_bio: Mr. Michael  Jardon | President, CEO & Executive Director | Age 55 | Compensation: $2.5M (FY2025)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 7K people. Revenue per employee of $230K ranks in the bottom quartile among Energy peers. Each employee generates $14K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $4K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 11× revenue per employee (reasonable relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags low compensation governance risk (1/10).
financial_summary: Expro Ltd is a small-cap energy business with a $1.5B market cap on $1.6B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +8% over the past three years, a respectable pace for a business of this size.

Returns on capital run at 3% against a 9% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, and 9% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $98M in free cash flow — roughly 6 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 4.07× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage runs at 8.1×.

Shareholder yield of 2.7% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.
